title: NHRC, India takessuo motucognizance of the reported snake bite of six girls leading to three deaths in a hostel in Gadchiroli district, Maharashtra
subtitle:
Reportedly, students slept on the floor due to lack of cots
The Commission issues a notice to the Maharashtra Chief Secretary, calling for a detailed report on the matter within two weeks
The report expected to include the health status of the injured
body_text:
The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India has taken suo motu cognizance of a media report that six girl students, belonging to the Scheduled Tribe, were bitten by a snake in a hostel of an Ashram school in Gadchiroli district, Maharashtra. Reportedly, they were sleeping on the floor inside their hostel room due to lack of cots. Three of the victim students succumbed to the snake bite, while the remaining three were undergoing treatment at a hospital.
The Commission has observed that the contents of the news report, if true, raise serious issues of violation of human rights. Therefore, it has issued a notice to the Maharashtra Chief Secretary, calling for a detailed report on the matter within two weeks. The report is expected to include the health status of the injured girl students.
According to the media report, carried on 11th August 2026, 79 girl students are accommodated in a single room of the hostel. The hostel, which has been functional for the last 25 years, lacks basic facilities. Every year, the district reports a significant number of snake bite cases.
***
NSK

enrichment.summary: The NHRC has taken suo motu cognizance of a media report that six Scheduled Tribe girl students were bitten by a snake at an Ashram school hostel in Gadchiroli district, Maharashtra, after being forced to sleep on the floor due to lack of cots; three of them died. The Commission issued a notice to the Maharashtra Chief Secretary seeking a detailed report within two weeks, including the health status of the injured, noting the report indicated 79 girls were housed in a single room in a 25-year-old hostel lacking basic facilities.
enrichment.context: The National Human Rights Commission derives its suo motu powers from the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, allowing it to take up cases of rights violations based on media reports without a formal complaint. Ashram schools are residential institutions run by state Tribal Welfare Departments (often under the Ministry of Tribal Affairs' broader framework) to provide education and boarding to children from Scheduled Tribe communities in remote, often forest-dwelling regions like Gadchiroli, which has historically poor infrastructure and high snakebite incidence. This incident highlights recurring concerns about overcrowding, inadequate infrastructure, and poor safety standards in tribal welfare hostels across India, issues that have been flagged in past NHRC and Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) reports on Ashram schools and Eklavya Model Residential Schools. Snakebite itself is a significant public health issue in India, which reports among the highest snakebite mortality globally, especially in rural and tribal belts; the government's National Action Plan for Prevention and Control of Snakebite Envenoming (NAPSE) was launched to address this but implementation gaps persist. The case underscores the intersection of tribal welfare administration, hostel/health infrastructure, and human rights accountability mechanisms.

prelims_questions.explanation: The NHRC was established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, which empowers it to take suo motu cognizance of human rights violations, including based on media reports.
